1.title: The Seven Guiding Principles
1.text: Welcome to Module nine: The Seven Guiding Principles. It covers the exam area The eye til Value System. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. List the seven guiding principles. Understand each principle and how it should be used. Describe how the principles interact and work together. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: The eye til Value System (forty percent). Exam format: forty multiple-choice questions in sixty minutes; twenty-six correct answers (sixty-five percent) pass. Validated against: the official eye til Foundation (Version five) syllabus, version five point zero (February two thousand twenty-six).

1.title: What the principles are
1.text: What the principles are. Guiding principles are recommendations that guide an organization in all circumstances, whatever its goals, strategy, type of work or structure. They are universal and enduring. There are seven.

1.title: What the principles are, continued
1.text: What the principles are. The figure shows this: The seven guiding principles.

1.title: What the principles are, continued
1.text: What the principles are. one. Principle: Focus on value. In one line: Everything must link back to value for stakeholders. two. Principle: Start where you are. In one line: Build on what exists; do not discard it without looking. three. Principle: Progress iteratively with feedback. In one line: Small steps, with feedback after each. four. Principle: Collaborate and promote visibility. In one line: Work together and make work visible.

1.title: What the principles are, continued
1.text: What the principles are. five. Principle: Think and work holistically. In one line: Look at the whole system, not one piece. six. Principle: Keep it simple and practical. In one line: Use the fewest steps needed for a useful result. seven. Principle: Optimize and automate. In one line: Improve first, then automate with technology. Exam tip: Learn the seven names in this order. Questions give a scenario and ask which principle it shows.

1.title: How to use each principle
1.text: How to use each principle. Focus on value. Know who the consumers are, what value means to them, and measure outcomes, not activity. Start where you are. Observe the current state directly, reuse what works, and measure before changing. Progress iteratively with feedback. Break work into pieces, improve in cycles, act on feedback, avoid a big-bang change. Collaborate and promote visibility. Involve the right people, share information, cross silos, show progress.

1.title: How to use each principle, continued
1.text: How to use each principle. Think and work holistically. Consider all four dimensions, the whole value chain and the wider context. Keep it simple and practical. Remove steps that add no value, prefer the simplest solution that works. Optimize and automate. Simplify and improve a process before automating it; use technology (including A I) where it helps people.

1.title: How the principles work together
1.text: How the principles work together. The principles do not stand alone. They are interrelated and often used together: for example, start where you are and focus on value tell you what to keep; progress iteratively and collaborate tell you how to change it; keep it simple stops over-design; optimize and automate comes last. No principle is more important, and all may be relevant at once. Typical trap: "automate everything first" breaks optimize and automate (improve first) and keep it simple. Exam tip: Scenario questions describe a mistake (big-bang change, hidden work, automating a bad process) and ask which principle was ignored. Name the opposite of the mistake. Exam tip: The principles are not ranked. Any option claiming one principle always comes first is wrong.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A team replaces its whole ticket tool at once, with no pilot and no feedback. Which principle did it ignore? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Progress iteratively with feedback. Big-bang change ignores small steps and feedback.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Before building a new knowledge base, the team reviews what already exists and reuses the best parts. Which principle is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Start where you are. The team builds on what exists.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Which statement about the guiding principles is C O R R E C T? (one) There are seven guiding principles. (two) They are used together and interact. (three) Only one principle applies at a time. (four) They apply only to I T operations. The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: one and two. Seven principles, used together.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Identify the missing word(s). The principle "blank" says to improve a process before automating it. The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Optimize and automate. Optimize first, then automate.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A department hides its work until it is finished and other teams cannot see progress. Which principle is it breaking? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Collaborate and promote visibility. Work should be shared and visible.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. An approval process has six sign-offs, but two add no value. Which principle suggests removing them? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Keep it simple and practical. Remove steps that add no value and keep it simple.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. A project looks only at technology and ignores people, suppliers and processes. Which principle is it breaking? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Think and work holistically. Holistic means considering all dimensions and the whole system.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. How many guiding principles are there? Answer: Seven. Question two. Name them. Answer: Focus on value; start where you are; progress iteratively with feedback; collaborate and promote visibility; think and work holistically; keep it simple and practical; optimize and automate. Question three. Which principle says everything should link back to value? Answer: Focus on value.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What should happen before automation? Answer: Optimize the process. Question five. Which principle warns against big-bang change? Answer: Progress iteratively with feedback. Question six. Is any principle more important than the others? Answer: No; they interact and are used together.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Principle: Cue. Focus on value: link everything to stakeholder value. Start where you are: observe and reuse. Progress iteratively with feedback: small steps, feedback. Collaborate and promote visibility: together and visible. Think and work holistically: whole system, four dimensions. Keep it simple and practical: remove what adds no value.
